note:
Six cards the rollout policy could not reach.

A player reported the bot walking into the same Marshal punish round after round. The bot's guess at the opponent's hand turned out to be exact — 30 comparisons of the sampler against the arithmetic, largest disagreement 2.26 standard errors — so it knew perfectly well how many Marshal coins were unaccounted for. What it could not do was play the card.

The heuristic ranks an action by the fields on it: a `target` makes it an attack, a `to` makes it a maneuver, anything else falls to `cleanup`, two drawers below a plain move. Six cards choose their target on a follow-up step and so carry neither field — the Marshal, the Ensign, the Earl, the Bishop, the Herald and the Footman. Measured over 120 games with every box out: offered 1401 times, played none. Not seldom. None. The Marshal's tactic is what makes a War Wagon dangerous to approach, and the Earl's claims a location, which is how the game is won.

Ranking them by what they do rather than by what fields they carry takes that class from 0% to 31.9%, which is where the `to`-shaped tactics already sit (34.1%). Two of the six stay at zero and should: the Bishop's and the Herald's plain equivalents — recruit and bolster — are themselves at the bottom of the chart.

This is a change to the rollout policy, and the rollout is the most sensitive part of this search: throwing its priority lists away costs 202 Elo, and adding 15% noise to it is worth +39. So the sign here is not guessable, and a better-playing policy is not automatically a better rollout. The reversal turns it off.

proposals.note: The old behaviour, written as a reversal because the fix is already in the code. A REJECT says the fix is worth having.
And the same on the base box alone, where four of the six cards live — the Marshal, the Ensign, the Bishop and the Footman. If the gain is real it should show without the expansions too.
